title: Ben Bohayin (or Bar Bohin)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: In Pesachim 57a: “Our Rabbis taught: Ben Bohayin gave pe’ah from vegetables; his father came and found the poor [with it]. He said to them: My sons, throw it away from you … not because my eye is stingy, but because the sages said one does not give pe’ah from vegetables.” In the Jerusalem Talmud there, end of chapter 4, this incident is cited, and he is called Ben Meivi Yayin. It also cites an incident about him: once the sages needed a donation, and they sent Rabbi Akiva and another with him. When they came to his house, they heard the boy asking him, “What shall we take today to eat?” and he instructed him to take the vegetables left over from yesterday, so as to buy cheaply. When they heard this they left without seeing him. Only after all the people had given their donations did they come to him, and he asked them why they had not come to him first. They told him what they had heard him instruct his boy, and he answered them: “What is between me and the boy you knew; what is between me and my Creator you did not. Nevertheless, since you came to me at the end, go to my wife and tell her, and she will give you a measure of dinars.” When they came to her she asked them whether her husband had commanded a leveled or heaped measure. They said to her, “He commanded without specifying.” She said: “I will give you heaped, and if it is against my husband’s wish, I will deduct it from my ketubah.” When her husband heard of her righteousness, he doubled her ketubah. The incident is cited in Esther Rabbah 2:3, and there he is called Barbuhin; in Tosefta Pesachim, end of chapter 3, he is called the son of Nevo.

notes.text: The Aramaic reply contrasts what the visitors know of his dealings with the boy with what they do not know of his relationship with his Creator. Its following instruction to the wife stays in the donor’s speech. Son/father, variant names, leveled/heaped measure, the wife’s possible ketubah deduction and the doubled ketubah are retained.

The consulted whole Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim chapter 4 passage at text[8][8] contains both the father/son vegetable notice and the complete donation narrative, including the boy/Creator contrast, wife’s heaped measure, possible ketubah deduction and doubled ketubah. The preliminary 4:1 substring hit was unrelated and excluded. Variant names across Esther Rabbah and Tosefta are reported, not independently merged.
